title_original: Faust review – FW Murnau’s silent masterpiece is a devilishly dazzling vision
editorial_title_zh: 《浮士德》影评——F·W·穆瑙的无声杰作是一场魔幻耀眼的视觉盛宴
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这部拍摄于1926年、改编自歌德悲剧故事的电影讲述了一个将灵魂卖给恶魔的男人的故事，至今仍是德国表现主义的一项壮丽成就。F·W·穆瑙于1926年推出的这部无声奇幻剧情片迎来了百年诞辰，这也让我们有机会细细品味这部神秘的电影，该片取材自歌德19世纪的……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "F·W·穆瑙于1926年推出的这部无声奇幻剧情片迎来了百年诞辰，这也让我们有机会细细品味这部神秘的电影，该片取材自歌德19世纪对炼金术士兼自然哲学家浮士德的描写：他将灵魂出卖给恶魔，但在德国浪漫主义高度崇高的最高潮中，他被爱所救赎。（确切地说，不是对上帝的爱，而是对一个好女人的爱；“爱”（Liebe）这个词最终出现在穆瑙由天堂唤起的同心圆交织愿景的中心，从而消除了他对恶魔的债务。）因此，它与克里斯托弗·马洛对《浮士德博士》那种更令人害怕、更残酷的描写有着很大的不同。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "穆瑙的《浮士德》显然关注并由邪恶所驱动，并且其中有着他四年前拍摄的《诺斯费拉图》的迴响。在这部电影中，浮士德在与梅菲斯特达成为期24小时的临时交易后，发现自己像吸血鬼一样害怕十字架。它也极具魏玛德国的电影特色，有着疯狂的能量以及耀眼的讽刺和黑色喜剧色彩；浮士德将所有死灵术卷轴连同《圣经》一同焚毁的烧书场景，与后来的历史事件产生了共鸣。（也许它间接启发了克劳斯·曼的小说《梅菲斯特》，该书后来被伊斯特凡·萨博拍成电影。）", "links": [{"text": "his Nosferatu", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2013/oct/24/nosferatu-eview"}, {"text": "Klaus Mann’s novel Mephisto, later to be filmed by István Szabó", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2025/dec/18/istvan-szabo-nazi-actor-mephisto"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "古斯塔夫·埃克曼（Gösta Ekman）饰演浮士德，他苍老而白发苍苍，宛如旧约先知（或如上帝本人），而资深演员埃米尔·詹宁斯（Emil Jannings，他在两年后凭借赢得第一届奥斯卡最佳男主角奖而创造了好莱坞历史）则饰演那个咧嘴笑、做鬼脸的梅菲斯特，他打赌自己能够败坏一个正派的人。当然，这个人就是浮士德，他为到处横行的瘟疫和满目疮痍感到痛苦，绝望地将自己博学的书本扔进火中，但随后被一页焦黑的书页吸引，上面讲述了如何在遥远的十字路口出卖你的灵魂。（这是否开启了蓝调音乐人罗伯特·约翰逊延续的传统？据传他曾做过类似的事情。）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "梅菲斯特向他提供他想要的一切，包括一场“酒神狂欢”或群交派对，并给了他一个与帕尔马公爵夫人——“意大利最美丽的女人”——厮混的机会。但浮士德最终还是想回到自己的家乡，变回曾经那个年轻的自己，并在那里爱上了美丽天真的格雷琴（卡米拉·霍恩饰），而梅菲斯特这位跳跃的无序之王，则与格雷琴风骚的玛特he姨妈（伊薇特·吉尔贝饰）打闹嬉戏。这一切将导致恐怖的结局，格雷琴因谋杀她与浮士德所生的孩子而被判处火刑，而浮士德本人则因在决斗中杀死了格雷琴愤怒的哥哥瓦伦丁（威廉·迪特勒，他后来成为获得奥斯卡奖的好莱坞导演）而遭到通缉。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《浮士德》的野心、规模和推动力是显而易见的：其中有一些精彩的模型特效，展现了浮士德和梅菲斯特俯瞰并飞越的风景与城市景观。而梅菲斯特作为一个巨大的邪恶天使、如同一朵巨大的云彩般盘旋在城市上空、用黑色的翅膀将其笼罩的静止画意画面，堪称神来之笔。", "translated": true}, article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "T he centenary of FW Murnau’s silent fantasy-melodrama from 1926 is the occasion to ponder this mysterious film, taken from Goethe’s 19th-century depiction of the alchemist and natural philosopher who sells his soul to the devil but, in a very high-minded climax of German romanticism, is redeemed by love. (Not love of God precisely, but love of a good woman; the word “Liebe” finally appears at the centre of Murnau’s radiating vision of concentric circles conjured by the heavens, which annul his debt to the Evil One.) It is therefore very different from Christopher Marlowe’s scarier and more unforgiving account of Doctor Faustus."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Murnau’s Faust is (obviously) concerned with and animated by evil, and there are echoes of his Nosferatu , made four years previously. In this film, Faust, having struck his bargain on a provisional 24-hour basis with Mephisto, finds that he is scared of a crucifix, like a vampire. It is also very much a film of Weimar Germany with its mad energy and streaks of garish satire and black comedy; the book-burning scene in which Faust immolates all his necromancy volumes, along with the Bible, is one which resonated with later events. (Perhaps it indirectly inspired Klaus Mann’s novel Mephisto, later to be filmed by István Szabó .)", "links": [{"text": "his Nosferatu", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2013/oct/24/nosferatu-eview"}, {"text": "Klaus Mann’s novel Mephisto, later to be filmed by István Szabó", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2025/dec/18/istvan-szabo-nazi-actor-mephisto"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Gösta Ekman plays Faust, ancient and grey-haired like an Old Testament prophet (or like God himself), and the veteran stager Emil Jannings (who, two years later, made Hollywood history by winning the first best actor Oscar) is the grinning, gurning Mephisto who makes a celestial wager that he can corrupt a decent man. This, of course, is Faust, who is wretched at the plague and devastation everywhere about and despairingly throws his learned books in the fire, but is then captivated by a charred page which tells of how to sell your soul at a distant crossroads. (Did this start the tradition carried on by bluesman Robert Johnson, who reputedly did something similar?)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mephisto offers him whatever he wants, including a “bacchanal” or orgy, and gives him an opportunity to dally with the Duchess of Parma, “the most beautiful woman in Italy”. article_text:
T he centenary of FW Murnau’s silent fantasy-melodrama from 1926 is the occasion to ponder this mysterious film, taken from Goethe’s 19th-century depiction of the alchemist and natural philosopher who sells his soul to the devil but, in a very high-minded climax of German romanticism, is redeemed by love. (Not love of God precisely, but love of a good woman; the word “Liebe” finally appears at the centre of Murnau’s radiating vision of concentric circles conjured by the heavens, which annul his debt to the Evil One.) It is therefore very different from Christopher Marlowe’s scarier and more unforgiving account of Doctor Faustus.

Murnau’s Faust is (obviously) concerned with and animated by evil, and there are echoes of his Nosferatu , made four years previously. In this film, Faust, having struck his bargain on a provisional 24-hour basis with Mephisto, finds that he is scared of a crucifix, like a vampire. It is also very much a film of Weimar Germany with its mad energy and streaks of garish satire and black comedy; the book-burning scene in which Faust immolates all his necromancy volumes, along with the Bible, is one which resonated with later events. (Perhaps it indirectly inspired Klaus Mann’s novel Mephisto, later to be filmed by István Szabó .)

Gösta Ekman plays Faust, ancient and grey-haired like an Old Testament prophet (or like God himself), and the veteran stager Emil Jannings (who, two years later, made Hollywood history by winning the first best actor Oscar) is the grinning, gurning Mephisto who makes a celestial wager that he can corrupt a decent man. This, of course, is Faust, who is wretched at the plague and devastation everywhere about and despairingly throws his learned books in the fire, but is then captivated by a charred page which tells of how to sell your soul at a distant crossroads. (Did this start the tradition carried on by bluesman Robert Johnson, who reputedly did something similar?)

Mephisto offers him whatever he wants, including a “bacchanal” or orgy, and gives him an opportunity to dally with the Duchess of Parma, “the most beautiful woman in Italy”. But Faust ultimately wants to go back to his home village as the young man he once was, and there falls in love with comely innocent Gretchen (Camilla Horn), while Mephisto, that capering lord of misrule, has knockabout high-jinks with Gretchen’s blowsy Aunt Marthe (Yvette Guilbert). It is to lead to horror, with Gretchen sentenced to be burned at the stake for murdering the child she conceived with Faust, who is in turn wanted for killing Gretchen’s outraged brother Valentin (William Dieterle, himself to become an Oscar-winning Hollywood director) in a duel.

The ambition, scale and drive of Faust are obvious: there is some wonderful model work for the landscape and cityscape that Faust and Mephisto look down on, flying above. And the still, painterly image of Mephisto as a vast evil angel, brooding over the city like a gigantic cloud, shrouding it in his black wings, is inspired.
